design_detail: Single-author critical review (accepted author manuscript, NIHMS518366) of 62 published quantitative studies of alcohol protective behavioral strategies (PBS) in college-student samples. Searches of APA PsycNet, Web of Science and Google Scholar with stated terms, plus reference lists and forward citations of the measure-development papers, ended in early February 2013. Narrative synthesis in four parts: how PBS were measured (Table 1: 11 measures and their variants), putative antecedents of PBS use, moderators of PBS–outcome relationships, and evidence for PBS as a mechanism of change; a one-line summary of each study in the Appendix. No protocol, no flow diagram, no per-study risk-of-bias appraisal and no pooling (the author states that a meta-analysis is still needed). Appraised with the editors' narrative-review checklist: the search is described, but the review has none of the other features of a systematic review.
can_establish: How alcohol protective behavioral strategies were defined and measured in college-student research up to February 2013, which measures had passed which psychometric tests, and which associations (antecedents, moderators, mediation in trials, within-person daily associations) had been reported, how often, and with what designs.
cannot_establish: Whether using any protective strategy reduces drinking or harm (the studies summarized are mostly cross-sectional, retrospective, self-reported and between-person, and no effect is pooled), how large any association is (sizes are printed for only a few studies), or whether the findings hold outside college students (non-college samples were excluded; countries of the samples are not reported).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Included studies used college-student samples, including incoming students and subgroups (student athletes, women, mandated students, lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender students), recruited as each study did (random samples from the National College Health Assessment, multi-university surveys, trial samples). Sources: APA PsycNet, Web of Science and Google Scholar searched with terms for protective behavioral strategies or drinking control strategies combined with alcohol or drinking; reference lists; studies citing any measure-development paper; searches ended early February 2013 (Identification of Studies, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Published quantitative studies in college-student samples whose measure unambiguously assessed PBS use and allowed PBS–variable relationships to be examined. Excluded: qualitative papers; non-college samples (few, and measured differently); measures limited to alcohol-avoidance strategies; PBS analysed only in combination with non-PBS variables (for example restraint or legal risk behaviours); PBS in other domains such as condom use (Identification of Studies, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not reported in aggregate. The Appendix describes most samples only in words (large, modest, small); counts are printed for a few, for example two halves of a five-university sample of 6139 and 6658 students who drank (Benton et al., 2008) and a 15-day diary study of 40 students (Pearson, D'Lima & Kelley, 2013) (Antecedents › PBS descriptive norms; Identifying Gaps › Recall bias).
sample.selection_effects: One author searched, selected and summarized; the search terms were those the author knew to describe PBS; no count of records screened or excluded and no flow diagram. Published studies only. Some studies held several samples and some samples appeared in several reports, so the number of independent samples is unknown (Identification of Studies, 2nd paragraph). Seven of the 62 studies are co-authored by the reviewer (editors' count: Appendix nos. 11, 18, 44–48), among them the only head-to-head comparison of measures, the response-scale study and the only daily-diary study, on which several of the review's judgments rest. Restriction to college students is described as pragmatic (Conclusion).

exposure.measurement: In the included studies, PBS use was self-reported on questionnaires: at least 11 measures (PBSS, NCHA, CAS, PSQ, PBSM, SQ, SCQ and four unnamed), most in several variants differing in number of items, response scale (contingent frequency, that is how often a strategy is used when drinking; absolute frequency; degree of truth; yes or no for a day or occasion) and time window (none stated for most PBSS studies; past 24 hours, past week, past 2 weeks, past 3 months, past 12 months, last school year, since arriving on campus) (Measurement of PBS, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. Strategies measured, as the review describes item content: setting a limit or leaving at a predetermined time; alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks; drinking water while drinking alcohol; eating before or during drinking; avoiding drinking games, mixing types of alcohol or keeping up with others; keeping track of drinks; using a designated driver or planning transport; going home with a friend; not leaving a drink unattended; asking a friend to say when one has had enough; and, in broad measures only, avoiding situations with alcohol (Protective Behavioral Strategies, 1st paragraph; Measurement of PBS › PBSS, PSQ, PBSM and SQ subsections).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed: the review concerns alcohol only, and other drug use in the included samples is not mentioned.

comparison.controls: No comparison group at review level. Designs summarized: mostly cross-sectional between-person correlations, regressions and mediation models; randomized trials of brief alcohol interventions in which PBS change was tested as a mediator (Larimer et al., 2007; Barnett et al., 2007; Murphy et al., 2012) or did not change (Kulesza et al., 2010; Neighbors et al., 2009; Walters et al., 2009); one experiment instructing students to drink less or to use more strategies (Sugarman & Carey, 2009); one assessment-reactivity experiment (Walters et al., 2009); panel and single-group pre–post studies; two studies separating within-person from between-person effects (Lewis et al., 2012; Pearson, D'Lima & Kelley, 2013).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review's own antecedent sections show that people who report more PBS differ in sex, drinking motives, personality and self-regulation, mental health and family history of alcoholism, all of which also relate to drinking; with mostly cross-sectional data, PBS use cannot be separated from these characteristics.

outcomes.instruments: Included studies: self-reported alcohol use (frequency, typical and heaviest quantity, heavy episodic drinking, estimated blood alcohol concentration) and alcohol-related problems (composite scales or single consequences such as injury or regretted acts). The review itself compares the measures' factor analyses (exploratory and confirmatory), response scales and time windows (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Only two measures have factor structures replicated in independent samples with both exploratory and confirmatory analyses: the PBSS (Martens et al., 2005) and the PSQ (DeMartini et al., 2013); the PBSM and the SQ failed a confirmatory analysis in an independent sample (Pearson, Kite & Henson, 2012a). Only one study tested measurement invariance by sex before comparing means (DeMartini et al., 2013) (Measurement of PBS › PBSM, SQ and Measurement summary; Antecedents › Gender).
outcomes.operationalization: PBS are conventionally defined by the harm they are presumed to reduce, a definition the author calls tautological. He proposes the narrow definition, strategies used immediately before, during or after drinking, and would treat avoidance of drinking as a separate, complementary construct (Measurement of PBS, 1st paragraph; Measurement summary; Conclusion).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no quantitative synthesis). The author notes that most antecedent and moderator findings come from single, unreplicated tests (Identifying Gaps in Knowledge, 1st paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooling. Numbers are printed for a few studies only: descriptive norms of PBS correlated with own PBS use r=.32 and .33 in two halves of a five-university sample (n=6139 and 6658; Benton et al., 2008); same-sex norms r=.35, .26 and .49 for the three PBSS subscales and opposite-sex norms r=.02, −.01 and −.08 (Lewis, Rees & Lee, 2009) (Antecedents › PBS descriptive norms); in LaBrie et al. (2011) the path from drinking motives to alcohol use fell from β=.58 to β=.17 when PBS were added, about 70% of the total effect (Antecedents › Drinking motives, 2nd paragraph). Most other findings are described as significant or not, without sizes or sample sizes.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at review level; covariates are named for some individual studies (for example gender and alcohol use).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The Appendix summarizes what the author judged the most distinctive significant PBS findings of each study, not all its findings, because PBS were not the main focus of every study (Summarizing the Nomological Network, 1st paragraph); non-significant results are therefore under-represented in the summaries.
analysis.power: Not applicable. The author notes that two of the three studies finding that PBS buffer the link between drinking and problems had samples large enough to detect very small interactions (Moderators › Alcohol use).

interpretation_gap.results_show: The PBS literature in college students up to February 2013 is mostly cross-sectional, retrospective, self-reported and between-person, and uses many variants of 11 measures. People who report more PBS report drinking less and fewer problems. In the two studies separating within-person from between-person effects, some strategies (the Serious Harm Reduction subscale, such as using a designated driver or going home with a friend, and day-to-day Limiting/Stopping) went with more drinking on the days they were used. PBS mediated intervention effects in three trials and did not change in three others, and an instruction to use more strategies raised reported strategy use without reducing drinking (one study).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and most of the discussion are cautious about designs, but the Conclusion ends by calling PBS use a promising way to reduce drinking and its negative consequences. The section on trials calls the three mediation findings some of the strongest evidence for a causal relationship between PBS use and alcohol outcomes (Review of Evidence › Randomized controlled trials), although PBS were not the randomized factor, were self-reported, and none of the interventions mainly targeted PBS (as the author concedes in Identifying Gaps › Weak tests of PBS use as a mechanism of change); the same paragraph argues that trials in which PBS did not change do not question the PBS–outcome relationship. The Highlights say PBS are consistently negatively correlated with alcohol-related problems, while the body reports positive associations for some strategies (daily-report studies; absolute-frequency scales; some items in Frank et al., 2012).

timeline.event: Prince, Carey & Maisto (2013) is cited as a recent methodological review of PBS measurement (Purpose of the Present Review); not read here.
Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials of protective behavioral strategies among adults, on the editors' reading list for this topic; not read or appraised here.

replication.where_it_stands: In 2013 the association between PBS and drinking was consistent between people but rested on cross-sectional self-report; within-person, prospective and experimental evidence was sparse and mixed. The author called for intensive longitudinal studies (daily diaries, ecological momentary assessment, objective alcohol measures) and a meta-analysis. A 2026 meta-analysis of randomized trials (Van Nhat et al.) addresses the trial evidence and should be read for the current state.

funding.funder: No official funding for the review; the author was supported by a National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism training grant, T32-AA018108 (Acknowledgments, 1st paragraph). A second acknowledgment sentence breaks off after the words supported in part by, with no funder named (Acknowledgments, 2nd paragraph).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the author manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: Center on Alcoholism, Substance Abuse, & Addictions, University of New Mexico. The author co-wrote 7 of the 62 included studies (editors' count), including the measure comparison (Pearson, Kite & Henson, 2012a), the response-scale study (Kite, Pearson & Henson, 2013) and the daily-diary study (Pearson, D'Lima & Kelley, 2013). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials that target one named strategy at a time (for example alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, or arranging a safe way home) against a control, with outcomes recorded at the event level in real time (daily diary or ecological momentary assessment with breath or transdermal alcohol) and harms such as injuries and blackouts as outcomes, in college and non-college samples; and a meta-analysis that separates within-person from between-person associations.

domains.note: Databases, terms, citation searching, end date and criteria are stated, which is more than most narrative reviews give; but one author did everything, the terms were those known to him, one of the three databases was Google Scholar, there is no count of records screened or excluded, and the exclusion of measures not unambiguously assessing PBS is a judgment.

No study-level appraisal, and sample and effect sizes are mostly not given; but the review appraises the measures' psychometric testing in detail and names the design problems that affect nearly all studies (cross-sectional between-person data, recall bias, common-method bias, weak tests of mediation).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Seven of 62 included studies are the author's; the judgments that the PBSS outperforms other measures, that absolute-frequency scales produce spurious positive correlations, and much of the within-person evidence come from them.

Limitations and the ecological fallacy are discussed explicitly, but trial mediation is described as among the strongest causal evidence, null trials are set aside as failures of method, and the final sentence calls PBS a promising way to reduce drinking.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a protective effect of PBS
domains.note: Counter-evidence (positive within-person associations, the null instruction experiment, trials that did not change PBS) is reported, but the framing favours a protective effect. Qualitative studies and non-college populations are excluded by design and so are not represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). This one is more transparent than most: its search is described and it is explicit about the weaknesses of the literature it summarizes. Its limits are a single reviewer, no study-level appraisal or effect sizes, reliance on the author's own studies for key judgments, and a conclusion more favourable than the designs allow. Had it been rated as a systematic review, AMSTAR 2 would give critically low confidence (no protocol, no risk-of-bias assessment of included studies). It may be cited for how PBS were measured, for the design profile of the literature to 2013 and for pointers to primary studies; claims about whether a strategy reduces harm should rest on the primary trials and on a systematic review of them, not on this review.

key_findings.finding: 62 published studies met the criteria; some contained more than one sample and some samples were reported in several papers, so the number of independent samples is unknown.

Search: APA PsycNet, Web of Science and Google Scholar, with terms for protective behavioral strategies or drinking control strategies combined with alcohol or drinking; reference lists; forward citations of measure-development studies; college samples only; qualitative studies excluded; searches ended early February 2013.

At least 11 PBS measures were used (PBSS, NCHA, CAS, PSQ, PBSM, SQ, SCQ and four unnamed), most in several variants of items, response scale and time window. The PBSS was the most used (36 studies, about 58%, in at least nine variants).
key_findings.locator: Measurement of PBS, 2nd paragraph; Table 1; Measurement of PBS › Variants of the PBSS, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The text's own subtotals for the PBSS (24 + 5 + 4 studies by time window) and the PBSS rows of Table 1 (33 listings) do not reach 36; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Only the PBSS and the PSQ have factor structures replicated in independent samples with both exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis; the PSQ in that form had been used in one published report. The PBSM and the SQ failed a confirmatory analysis in an independent sample.
key_findings.locator: Measurement of PBS › Measurement summary; PBSM; SQ

key_findings.finding: The response scale changes the direction of results: with an absolute-frequency scale (number of times a strategy was used), the SQ subscale of strategies used while drinking correlated positively with drinking, because it also counts drinking occasions; with a contingent-frequency scale (how often when drinking), correlations were negative (Kite, Pearson & Henson, 2013, three studies).
key_findings.locator: Measurement of PBS, 3rd paragraph; Measurement of PBS › SQ

key_findings.finding: 13 of the 62 studies (about 21%) used a broad definition that includes avoiding drinking altogether; the author recommends the narrow definition (strategies used immediately before, during or after drinking).
key_findings.locator: Measurement of PBS › Broad vs. narrow operational definition; Conclusion

key_findings.finding: Women reported more PBS than men in nearly every study that compared them; only four studies reported any non-significant sex difference, and only one tested whether the measure worked the same way in both sexes before comparing means.

Perceived norms of PBS use predicted own PBS use: r=.32 and .33 in two halves of a five-university sample (n=6139 and 6658); same-sex norms r=.35, .26 and .49 across the three PBSS subscales, opposite-sex norms r=.02, −.01 and −.08; both held in regressions adjusted for sex, drinking and problems (the review does not state these two studies' designs).
key_findings.locator: Antecedents/Predictors of PBS Use › PBS descriptive norms

key_findings.finding: Three cross-sectional studies found that PBS use statistically mediated part of the link between some drinking motives (for example social and enhancement motives) and drinking or problems, motives going with lower PBS use; in LaBrie et al. (2011) the motives–alcohol use path fell from β=.58 to β=.17 with PBS in the model (about 70% of the total effect). The author notes that cross-sectional data do not allow full tests of mediation.
key_findings.locator: Antecedents/Predictors of PBS Use › Drinking motives, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: In three studies, people reporting more PBS showed a weaker association between how much they drank and their problems (Benton et al., 2004, 2006; Borden et al., 2011). Other moderators (mental and physical health, refusal self-efficacy, motives, negative urgency, self-esteem, self-regulation) come mostly from single studies; the author calls the pattern of stronger associations in higher-risk groups very preliminary.
key_findings.locator: Moderators of the Relationships between PBS Use and Alcohol-Related Outcomes › Alcohol use; Health variables; Other variables

key_findings.finding: Trials: in three randomized trials of brief interventions with college students, change in PBS statistically mediated the intervention's effect on drinking or problems (Larimer et al., 2007, mailed personalized feedback, 12 months, an effect described as fully mediated; Barnett et al., 2007, brief motivational interview with mandated students, PBS at 3 months and drinks per day at 12 months, per drinking day in the Appendix; Murphy et al., 2012, small trial with a behavioral economic supplement, 6 months). In three other trials the intervention did not change PBS (Kulesza et al., 2010; Neighbors et al., 2009; Walters et al., 2009). None of the interventions mainly targeted PBS.
key_findings.locator: Review of Evidence for PBS as a Mechanism of Change › Randomized controlled trials; Identifying Gaps in Knowledge › Weak tests of PBS use as a mechanism of change

key_findings.finding: Students instructed to use more strategies reported using more, but their drinking did not fall, and changes in strategy use were not correlated with changes in drinking (Sugarman & Carey, 2009). Students assessed at baseline and at 3, 6 and 12 months reported more PBS and less drinking than students assessed only at 12 months, suggesting that being asked about PBS changes reports (Walters et al., 2009).
key_findings.locator: Review of Evidence for PBS as a Mechanism of Change › Other experimental designs

key_findings.finding: Longitudinal studies without randomization gave mixed results: after a brief intervention, strategy use rose at 6 weeks but its change was not correlated with drinking outcomes (Martens et al., 2007, single group); in data from a peer intervention that had no significant effect (Cimini et al., 2009, analysed by Martens et al., 2011; baseline, 6 and 12 months), prospective correlations with drinking were similar to the cross-sectional ones while those with problems were weaker (3 of 9 non-significant); with the other subscales controlled, change in Manner of Drinking strategies predicted fewer drinks per week and change in Serious Harm Reduction strategies predicted alcohol problems at 6 and 12 months (direction not stated in the text; Appendix no. 35 says changes in two of the three subscales predicted less use or problems), and change in each subscale correlated negatively with change in one to three alcohol outcomes (Appendix no. 7); in women, strategy use did not predict drinking or problems at the same time point (baseline or 4 months), but baseline use predicted fewer problems 4 months later, adjusted for age, baseline problems, quantity and frequency of drinking and risk-amplifying behaviours (Luebbe et al., 2009).
key_findings.locator: Review of Evidence for PBS as a Mechanism of Change › Non-experimental longitudinal designs; Appendix nos. 7, 31 and 35

key_findings.finding: Within-person evidence (two studies: 7-day recall around the 21st birthday, Lewis et al., 2012; 15-day daily diary of 40 students, Pearson, D'Lima & Kelley, 2013): Manner of Drinking strategies went with less drinking both between people and on the days used; on days when Limiting/Stopping strategies were used, people drank more; Serious Harm Reduction strategies (such as a designated driver or going home with a friend) went with more drinking between people and on the days used, and with more problems on those days. The author suggests such strategies may be used mainly when heavy drinking is planned.
key_findings.locator: Review of Evidence for PBS as a Mechanism of Change › Designs with daily PBS reports

key_findings.finding: Nearly all included studies measured both PBS and outcomes by retrospective self-report, often with no time window; three studies limited recall to one occasion or used a daily diary (Frank et al., 2012; Neighbors et al., 2009; Pearson, D'Lima & Kelley, 2013).
key_findings.locator: Identifying Gaps in Knowledge › Recall bias
key_findings.note: The abstract says two such studies; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: The abstract states that 80% of the 62 reports gave only cross-sectional data and that two studies examined both within-person and between-person effects.
key_findings.note: The 80% figure is not derived anywhere in the body or Appendix; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: The author concludes that intervention, experimental and longitudinal studies give mixed evidence for PBS as a mediator of intervention effects and as a prospective predictor of outcomes, calls for intensive longitudinal designs and a meta-analysis, and ends by calling PBS use a promising way to reduce drinking and its consequences.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion; Identifying Gaps in Knowledge › Moving forward

key_findings.finding: The author's own summary of the cross-sectional evidence: nearly every reviewed study supports that students who report using more strategies also report drinking less and/or fewer alcohol-related problems (negative correlations with drinking frequency, quantity, heavy episodes, estimated blood alcohol concentration and problem measures, with examples cited); he calls the support for these negative correlations between self-reported strategy use and self-reported drinking or problems strong, and the Highlights say strategy use is consistently negatively correlated with problems. No effect sizes are given.
key_findings.locator: Protective Behavioral Strategies, 2nd paragraph; Purpose of the Present Review, 1st paragraph; Highlights
key_findings.note: The body also reports positive associations for some strategies (daily-report studies, absolute-frequency scales), so 'consistently' in the Highlights overstates (see interpretation gap).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says only two studies tried to reduce recall bias, but the Recall bias section names three (Frank et al., 2012 and Neighbors et al., 2009, single occasion; Pearson, D'Lima & Kelley, 2013, daily diary).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the body's count of three, with its named studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's figure that 80% of the 62 reports gave only cross-sectional data is not derived in the body, and the Appendix does not state each study's design consistently. An editors' rough count of Appendix summaries that describe a trial, experiment, follow-up or daily design gives 14 to 16 of 62 (about 74–77% otherwise).
reporting_issues.consequence: The proportion cannot be checked exactly; cite it as the author's estimate (about three-quarters to four-fifths of studies cross-sectional), not as a verified count.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 36 studies (about 58%) used the PBSS, with 16 using a 5-point and 15 a 6-point scale, and by time window 24 with none stated, 5 with 3 months and 4 with a single day or occasion. The time-window subtotals add to 33, the scale subtotals plus the 4 yes/no studies to 35, and Table 1's PBSS rows list 33 (16 five-point, 13 six-point, 4 yes/no).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the number of PBSS studies is between 33 and 36. Cite as about 33 to 36 or as the author's figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The note to Table 1 says studies with a factor analysis are in bold and scale-development papers are underlined, but the PMC author manuscript renders neither mark (the HTML table contains no bold or underline).
reporting_issues.consequence: These two attributes can be read from this version only through the Factor Analysis column and the text.

reporting_issues.issue: Citation inconsistencies: Novik & Boekeloo appears once as 2012 (Measurement of PBS, 4th paragraph) but as 2011 elsewhere and in the reference list; Nguyen et al. is 2011 in the text and Table 1 but 2010 in the Appendix, with two co-authors' names spelled inconsistently (Wyatt or Syatt; DeJong or DeLong). A moderation finding on drinking refusal self-efficacy (Moderators › Other variables) is reported without naming its study (the Appendix attributes it to Ehret, Ghaidarov & LaBrie, 2013).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; check the primary paper's year and identity before citing any of these through the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The second paragraph of the Acknowledgments ends mid-sentence after the words supported in part by, with no funder named.
reporting_issues.consequence: The funding statement of the author manuscript may be incomplete; the published version was not read.

disagreements.first_pass: Longitudinal studies without randomization gave mixed results: after a brief intervention PBS rose at 6 weeks but change was not correlated with drinking outcomes (Martens et al., 2007); prospective correlations with problems were weaker than cross-sectional ones, 3 of 9 non-significant (Martens et al., 2011); in women, PBS were unrelated to drinking at the same time point but baseline PBS predicted fewer problems 4 months later (Luebbe et al., 2009). (locator: Review of Evidence for PBS as a Mechanism of Change › Non-experimental longitudinal designs)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 271 (blind second reading): confirmed, with refinements: in Luebbe et al. (2009) strategies were unrelated to both drinking and problems at the same time point (baseline and 4 months); in Martens et al. (2011) prospective correlations with drinking were similar to the cross-sectional ones. 'Missed': change-score findings favouring strategies (Cimini et al., 2009, Appendix no. 7; Manner of Drinking change predicting fewer drinks per week at 6 and 12 months, Martens et al., 2011).
disagreements.resolution: All confirmed in the saved PMC text (Non-experimental longitudinal designs, 1st paragraph; Appendix nos. 7, 31, 35); the finding now carries the refinements and the favourable change-score results, with the Serious Harm Reduction direction marked as unstated in the body.

disagreements.first_pass: Trials: in three randomized trials of brief interventions with college students, change in PBS statistically mediated the intervention's effect on drinking or problems (Larimer et al., 2007, mailed personalized feedback, 12 months; Barnett et al., 2007, brief motivational interview with mandated students, PBS at 3 months and drinks per day at 12 months, per drinking day in the Appendix; Murphy et al., 2012, small trial with a behavioral economic supplement, 6 months). In three other trials the intervention did not change PBS (Kulesza et al., 2010; Neighbors et al., 2009; Walters et al., 2009). None of the interventions mainly targeted PBS.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 271 (blind second reading): confirmed; refinement: the body says Larimer et al.'s effect was fully mediated.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed (Review of Evidence › Randomized controlled trials, 1st paragraph); added.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 271 (blind second reading), 'missed': no key finding records the review's own summary of the cross-sectional evidence (nearly every study: more strategies, less drinking and/or fewer problems); the claim omits it.
disagreements.resolution: True and it matters (the claim cl_alc_protective_strategies understated it); checked at the stated places and added as the last key finding so that earlier indexes do not move.
